problems.title: Kernels of maximum-degree representations
problems.description: Can the largest irreducible representations collectively detect every element of a finite p-group?
problems.statement: Let G be a finite p-group, and let p^e be the largest degree of an irreducible complex representation of G. If p > e, must the intersection of the kernels of all irreducible representations of degree p^e be {1}?
problems.statement_latex: For a finite $p$-group $G$, set $p^e=\max_{\chi\in\operatorname{Irr}_{\mathbb C}(G)}\chi(1)$. Does $p>e$ imply $\bigcap_{\chi(1)=p^e}\ker\chi=\{1\}$?
details: The degree of a representation is its dimension. The question asks whether the representations of largest degree, taken together, distinguish every nonidentity group element.
The intersection ranges over every ordinary irreducible complex representation of that maximum degree.
scope: The integer e is the logarithm to base p of the largest character degree; it is not the exponent of G.
Collective faithfulness does not require a single faithful irreducible representation.
A proof for a restricted family of groups must retain that restriction.

problems.title: Simple twisted group algebras
problems.description: Must a finite group be soluble if one of its twisted group algebras over an arbitrary field is simple?
problems.statement: Let G be a finite group, let K be any field, and let α be a normalized 2-cocycle with values in K×. If the twisted group algebra K^α G is simple, must G be soluble?
problems.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a finite group, $K$ a field, and $\alpha:G\times G\to K^\times$ a normalized $2$-cocycle. If $K^\alpha G$ is simple, must $G$ be soluble?
details: The twisted group algebra has a K-basis indexed by G, with multiplication u_g u_h = α(g,h)u_gh. The cocycle identity ensures associativity.
Simple means that the algebra has no nonzero proper two-sided ideals. Its center is not required to equal K.

The AI generated manuscript proposes a full affirmative answer, covering characteristic zero and positive characteristic. It is available before human review, with its original verification notice intact.
scope: G is finite and K is arbitrary; no splitting-field or algebraic-closure assumption may be added.
Simplicity and central simplicity are distinct. The editors identify the central-simple case as known.
Soluble and solvable mean the same group-theoretic property.
A public proposed solution does not establish that the original problem has been settled.

problems.title: Augmentation ideals and the Jacobson radical
problems.attribution: I. Kaplansky · contributed by D. S. Passman
problems.description: When does the augmentation ideal of a group algebra coincide with its Jacobson radical?
problems.statement: For an arbitrary field K and a nontrivial group G, is J(K[G]) = I_K(G) equivalent to the existence of a prime p such that char K = p and G is a locally finite p-group?
problems.statement_latex: For a field $K$ and a nontrivial group $G$, is $J(K[G])=I_K(G)$ equivalent to $\operatorname{char}K=p>0$ and $G$ being a locally finite $p$-group?
details: The augmentation map sends a finite sum of group elements with coefficients in K to the sum of those coefficients. Its kernel is the augmentation ideal I_K(G).
The Jacobson radical is the intersection of the maximal right ideals. A group is locally finite if every finitely generated subgroup is finite.
scope: The group must be nontrivial; for the trivial group both ideals vanish in every characteristic.
K[G] denotes the ordinary group algebra, not a completion.
Elementwise p-power torsion alone does not assert local finiteness.

problems.title: Infinite groups of exponent five
problems.description: Can a finitely generated group be infinite if the fifth power of every element is the identity?
problems.statement: Does there exist an infinite finitely generated group G such that x^5 = 1 for every element x of G? Equivalently, is the free Burnside group B(d,5) infinite for some finite d ≥ 2?
problems.statement_latex: Does there exist a group $G=\langle g_1,\ldots,g_d\rangle$, for some finite $d\ge2$, such that $|G|=\infty$ and $x^5=1$ for every $x\in G$? Equivalently, is $B(d,5)$ infinite for some finite $d\ge2$?
details: Finite generation is essential: the question requires a fixed finite set of generators.
The identity must hold for every group element, including every word in the generators.
scope: This is part (b), which fixes exponent five.
The full Burnside group and the restricted Burnside group are different objects.
A negative answer must address every finite generating rank; checking rank two alone is insufficient.

preprints.title: Simple twisted group algebras over arbitrary fields
preprints.attribution_note: The mathematical argument and manuscript were generated by ChatGPT. The seminar has not yet reviewed this version. The supplied manuscript does not list human authors.
preprints.abstract: A proposed affirmative answer to Kourovka Problem 18.78 for arbitrary fields. The manuscript combines character-theoretic transitivity under group and Galois automorphisms, an affine reduction, and a characteristic-two argument. Galois descent and Witt-vector lifting connect the character theorem to simple twisted group algebras.
preprints.statement: For every finite group G, every field K, and every normalized 2-cocycle α: G × G → K×, simplicity of K^α G implies that G is soluble.
preprints.review_summary: Two separate AI agents reviewed this manuscript on 6 November 2026: one examined the character-theoretic core, and the other examined the Galois, Brauer-character, and field-descent arguments. Neither reported a decisive flaw in the parts examined. The review notes record the scope and limitations of these AI checks.
